Colophon · How this was made

The whole thing is
just files.

No framework. No bundler. No npm install. No build step at all. You could download this folder, double-click index.html, and every particle, every note, every physics ball would run from your hard drive, offline. That constraint is the argument — so here's exactly how it's put together.

01 / The receipts

Counted live, in the page

measuring…

That number is this site's own hand-written source, fetched and measured by JavaScript running right now. The mid-2020s average web page ships several megabytes. Everything you've experienced here — the flow field, the synth, the physics, the scroll story — fits in a rounding error, because there's no framework tax to pay.

02 / Under the hood

Three folders, zero dependencies

The site is three HTML pages sharing one stylesheet and three small JavaScript modules. That's the entire dependency graph. Here is what each piece does and why it exists.

The structure

  • index.html — the manifesto and the six headline live demos
  • possible.html — the capability catalogue, mini previews, and the honest scorecard
  • about.html — this colophon (the flex)
  • css/style.css — every style, hand-written, custom-property themed
  • js/engine.js — shared chrome plus reusable primitives: a seeded RNG, a value-noise field, HiDPI canvas fitting, and an on-screen render loop
  • js/demos.js — the interactive widgets, each self-mounting onto a data-demo element
  • js/story.js — the scroll-choreographed constellation scene

The techniques on display

  • Flow-field particles — a few hundred agents advected through a value-noise field on the <canvas> 2D context, steered toward your cursor.
  • Verlet physics — position-based dynamics with pairwise collision resolution and drag-to-fling, in about sixty lines.
  • Web Audio synthesis — every note is two detuned oscillators with an exponential gain envelope, summed through a master gain. No audio files exist in this project.
  • Seeded generative art — a mulberry32 PRNG means each artwork is reproducible from a 32-bit seed, so "billions of pieces" is literally true.
  • Scroll choreography — an IntersectionObserver activates steps while a sticky canvas reads scroll progress to assemble a 3D point cloud.
  • Custom cursor & magnetic fields — pointer events feed a spring system; the bespoke cursor uses mix-blend-mode: difference so it reads on any background.

The bit we're proud of

Every animation respects prefers-reduced-motion. If your system asks for calm, the flow field paints a single static frame, the physics settles instantly, the marquees stop, and the demos still show what they are — they just don't move. Accessibility isn't a separate mode bolted on; it's a branch inside each module. Render loops also pause when their canvas scrolls off-screen, so the page doesn't cook your battery.

If a website is the message, then hand-building one that does all this — in plain files, offline-capable, framework-free — is the whole argument, delivered without saying a word.

A genuine word for the blocks

We'll say it one more time, plainly: page-builders and block editors are some of the best things to happen to the web. They put publishing in the hands of people who shouldn't have to learn a render loop to launch a bakery. Most of the web should be blocks. We are fans.

This little site only exists to wave from the other side of the fence — to point at the more that the browser has always quietly offered, and to do it the cheekiest way we know how: by being made of exactly the stuff it's bragging about. Thanks for poking the demos. Now go build something that listens back.

Go ahead — poke it again.

The demos don't get tired. Head back to the showcase, fling some balls, play a chord, and roll a few hundred generative artworks no one has ever seen.
